card.title: Electric Currents, Drift Velocity and Current

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **Electric current** is the rate of charge flow, I = Q/t, measured in amperes (C/s), flowing (by convention) as positive charge would — opposite to electron motion. The electrons themselves drift: random thermal motion at ~10⁶ m/s acquires a tiny average **drift velocity** v_d (~10⁻⁴ m/s) along the wire.…

rows.text: - I = Q/t; 1 A = 1 C/s - I = neAv_d - J = I/A = nev_d

rows.text: **Drift speed ≠ signal speed:** electrons crawl at ~0.1 mm/s, but the field (and the lamp) responds at near light speed.  ·  **Current is a scalar** with a direction convention — not a true vector like force.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Charge per second, not speed** — the ampere counts electrons passing a point.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: I = Q/t (ampere); I = neAv_d; drift speed ~10⁻⁴ m/s.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The random thermal speed of electrons (~10⁶ m/s) is a trillion times the drift speed — the drift is a tiny bias on chaos.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Surprisingly Slow Electron March Flip a switch and the lamp lights instantly — yet the electrons themselves drift at less than a millimetre per second. Current is not speed but *charge per second*: I = neAv_d links the micro-world of drifting electrons to the amperes of a circuit.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024) ### 2.1 Electric current **Current** is the rate of flow of electric charge: $$I = \frac{Q}{t} \qquad \text{SI unit: ampere (A) = C/s}$$ - Conventional current flows in the direction positive charges would move (opposite to electron motion). - Current is a **scalar** with direction convention — it adds algebraically at junctions.…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 99:** the drift motion meets lattice resistance — Ohm's law's microscopic origin. - **To current density:** J = I/A = nev_d, a vector version. - **To fields:** the driving field E inside the wire relates to v_d via mobility: v_d = μE.
